synthesis: This lecture presents computational neuroscience as a research strategy, not a particular software package, algorithm, or job title. The strategy may start from data and estimate neural representations, or start from a mechanistic hypothesis and build a model for simulation. Its essential standards are clear variables, computable predictions, falsifiable assumptions, and results that answer a neuroscience question. Later lectures apply this language to single neurons, population coding, vision, movement, decision-making, reinforcement learning, and memory.
commonTraps: Equating computational neuroscience with “using computers” or “training neural networks.”
Assuming that a good fit proves the proposed mechanism; different models can make similar predictions.
Choosing a tool before defining the question, leaving variables, units, and falsifiable predictions unspecified.
Treating firing rate as a directly observed continuous quantity even though it is usually a statistical estimate.
Treating course logistics as permanent academic content; Page 3 belongs to the 2025 course archive.
This lecture establishes only the concepts and dependencies needed by the next 26 lectures; it is not a general survey of computational neuroscience.

Lines 1-3 — Workspace: clear all makes the course environment reproducible but also clears the function cache; it has no mathematical reset effect. For routine work, prefer clearvars; close all; clc. Lines 8-14 — Objects and scalar expansion: s + A relies on MATLAB scalar expansion. This is valid MATLAB syntax, but it is not abstract matrix addition between unequal shapes. Lines 17-22 — Sums and products: sum(A) reduces columns by default; u*v is dimensionally undefined, whereas u*v' is an outer product. Always state the output shape. Lines 25-29 — Matrix products: A*v, B*u, A*B, and B*A are governed by matching inner dimensions. Predict shape before execution and interpret only defined products. Lines 32-44 — Inverses, determinants, and singularity: the script demonstrates explicit inversion for B. In numerical work, use a linear solve. C is singular because det(C)=0; inv(C) is not a mathematical inverse. A determinant alone is not a stable numerical singularity test. Lines 47-54 — Hadamard products: A.*A is elementwise and differs from A*A. Similar symbols denote different algebras.
synthesis: This lecture establishes the grammar used by almost every later formula: first identify whether each object is a scalar, vector, or matrix and determine its shape; then decide whether the operation is defined. The probability material moves from univariate Bernoulli and exponential distributions to bivariate Gaussians, marginals, conditionals, and Bayes' rule. An expression that MATLAB can execute is not necessarily an operation defined in abstract mathematics, so program output must be interpreted separately from the meaning of its objects.
commonTraps: Mistaking MATLAB scalar expansion for scalar+matrix addition in abstract linear algebra.
Confusing * with .*: the former is matrix multiplication, whereas the latter is a Hadamard product.
Calculating entries before checking shape and thereby assigning a result to an undefined operation.
Treating a density value as the probability of one exact value of a continuous variable.
Assuming that uncorrelated variables are always independent; this implication holds only in special cases such as a Gaussian distribution.
Reversing the conditioning directions of posterior, likelihood, and prior.

Interpreting clear all and inv in the MATLAB source literally as best practices. Numerical work generally favors solving a linear system over forming an explicit inverse. Keep MATLAB's scalar-plus-matrix behavior distinct from abstract linear algebra.

Lines 1-3 — Reset: clear all is pedagogically harmless but heavier than clearvars; it does not change the model. Lines 7-15 — Time grid and parameters: t0 is a time shift or onset, not a frequency. The source comment conflicts with its use. Units are seconds. Lines 17-30 — Piecewise input: the strict condition < 0.250 leaves I(end)=NaN at T=0. The state may input 250; use a final else or <=. It can remain finite because Euler uses I(i-1), but the input plot loses its endpoint. Lines 32-44 — Euler integration: x(i)=x(i-1)+dt*(-x(i-1)+I(i-1))/tau is explicit Euler evaluated from the previous state and right-hand side. Check dt/tau and units. Lines 48-61 — Second-order conversion: the harmonic oscillator is implemented as x'=y and y'=-x with two first-order updates. The state vector is conceptually 2×1. Lines 63-69 — Numerical behavior: explicit Euler has update eigenvalues 1±i dt with modulus >1, so the orbit slowly spirals outward. This numerical instability is not biological energy input.
synthesis: A differential equation defines a full time trajectory through a local rate of change, while an initial condition selects one member of the solution family. An analytic solution exposes exact structure and enables limiting checks; Euler's method turns the derivative definition into an iterative update. A numerical result is trustworthy only when the step size is appropriate relative to the time constant, not merely because the code runs. Higher-order equations can be rewritten as coupled first-order systems by adding state variables, which is foundational for later network dynamics.
commonTraps: Treating a derivative as the total change over a finite interval instead of the instantaneous rate obtained as Δt→0.
Dropping the initial condition or integration constant when solving by separation of variables.
Assuming that executable code implies a sufficiently small Δt.
An Euler update evaluates I(t_n), not the unknown I(t_{n+1}); an off-by-one index changes the algorithm.
Confusing the exact oscillatory dynamics with the outward spiral produced by explicit Euler.
Confusing the time constant τ with the simulation step Δt.
A code explanation must connect every MATLAB line to its differential equation, discrete update, and plotted result; potential bugs and incorrect source comments must be listed separately.

synthesis: The Dirac delta makes each spike time an integrable event, and convolution of a synaptic kernel with a spike train produces a continuous current. In the large-N limit, a proposed weight scaling must be checked for both mean and variance. Scaling as 1/N keeps the mean finite but suppresses fluctuations to zero. Balanced 1/√N scaling lets large excitation and inhibition cancel in the mean while preserving O(1) fluctuations.
commonTraps: Treating δ(t) as an ordinary infinite number at t=0.
Reversing the time direction of K(t−t') and K(t') in a convolution.

Checking only mean scaling and not variance scaling.
Interpreting E/I balance as exact equality of excitation and inhibition at every instant.
The scaling derivations in this lecture are easy to distort by skipping steps. Calculate mean and variance separately and state the independence assumption explicitly.

synthesis: The solution of a first-order linear ODE is the causal exponential convolution of its past input; conversely, exponential convolution can be implemented by an ODE with one additional state variable. This equivalence turns a spiking network into a coupled voltage-and-current system and, under temporal averaging and timescale separation, produces rate models. Different rate-model forms make different assumptions about which variables are fast or slow and cannot be interchanged merely because they look similar.
